lead: A convolutional network learns its own features. Instead of hand-designed descriptors such as HOG or SIFT, it stacks small trainable filters and lets gradient descent decide what they detect. Depth buys accuracy, but plain deep stacks stop improving, so residual connections keep them trainable. These backbones sit under phone photo tagging, medical screening, and every detector later in this unit.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 for convolution, stride and padding, and 6.2 for the classifier idea that softmax and cross-entropy replace.

sections.h3: A convolution layer learns its own filters

blocks.text: An image enters as n × n pixels with C channels, three for colour. A convolution layer holds F filters, each a k × k × C block of weights. Every filter slides across the image and produces one output map, so the layer outputs F channels. The same weights are reused at every position — weight sharing — so a 3 × 3 filter learns 9 numbers per input channel, not one per pixel. Each output value sees only a k × k patch of the input: its local receptive field.

blocks.where: n is the input side in pixels, k the kernel side, s the stride in pixels per step, p the padding in pixels added on each side, and ⌊·⌋ is the floor. For a square input the same value applies to both sides.

blocks.text: After each convolution comes a ReLU, max(0, x), which keeps positive sums and zeroes negatives. A 2 × 2 max pool with stride 2 keeps the largest of four values, halving each side. Stacking conv–ReLU–pool grows the receptive field and shrinks the map, so filters become hierarchical: early layers fire on edges and colour blobs, middle layers on textures, deep layers on object parts and whole objects.

Fully connected layers flatten the last maps and mix them. A softmax turns final scores z into probabilities, ŷ_c = exp(z_c) ÷ Σ_j exp(z_j), and training minimises cross-entropy L = −Σ_c y_c log ŷ_c, where y_c is 1 for the true class and 0 for the rest, and ŷ_c is the predicted probability of class c.

AlexNet (2012) took a 227 × 227 × 3 image through 5 convolution layers and 3 fully connected layers to 1000 ImageNet classes. The first layer used 96 filters of 11 × 11 with stride 4. Three choices made it train: ReLU instead of sigmoid, dropout with rate 0.5 on the two large fully connected layers, and heavy augmentation — random crops, flips, colour jitter — over 1.2 million images. It held about 60 million parameters and was split across two GPUs. ZFNet kept the same layout and shrank the first-layer kernels to 7 × 7 with stride 2 after visualising them; a tuning win, not a new idea.

VGG repeats one pattern: every convolution is 3 × 3, stride 1, padding 1, so size is unchanged; every pool is 2 × 2, stride 2, so size halves. VGG-16 is 13 convolution plus 3 fully connected layers; VGG-19 is 16 plus 3. Two 3 × 3 convolutions see a 5 × 5 region and three see 7 × 7, with fewer weights and more ReLUs than one wide kernel. Almost all parameters sit in the first fully connected layer: 7 × 7 × 512 = 25,088 inputs into 4096 units is about 102.8 million weights, the bulk of roughly 138 million.

sections.h3: ResNet: the shortcut that made depth work

blocks.text: Plain networks got worse as they got deeper: training error rose too, which is degradation, not overfitting. A residual block learns a correction. Its output is y = F(x) + x, where x is the block input, F(x) is what two or three convolution layers compute, and y is the result. If the best behaviour is to do nothing, F only needs pushing to zero, which is easy. The identity shortcut carries x with no weights, so the block adds no parameters whenever the shapes match; only the projection shortcut adds a 1 × 1 convolution.

Batch normalisation follows each convolution: it rescales activations to zero mean and unit variance, then applies a learned scale and shift, which allows higher learning rates. When the shortcut crosses a channel change or a stride-2 downsample, a 1 × 1 convolution with matching stride projects x to the right shape. For 50, 101 and 152 layers the block is a bottleneck — 1 × 1 conv to shrink channels, 3 × 3 conv, 1 × 1 conv to restore — and the family runs from 18 to 152 layers (18, 34, 50, 101, 152). Gradients pass through the sum node, which eases the vanishing-gradient problem.
Inception, or GoogLeNet, runs several filter sizes in parallel inside one block and concatenates the outputs. DenseNet connects each layer to every later layer's input.

sections.h3: Recognition versus verification, and newer backbones

blocks.text: Recognition names the class of one image. Verification answers a yes/no question: are these two images the same identity? A Siamese network runs two copies of one CNN with shared weights and compares the two embeddings. Contrastive loss pulls a matching pair together and pushes a non-matching pair apart until a margin is reached.

blocks.where: d⁺ = ||f(a) − f(p)||₂ is the distance between an anchor a and a positive p of the same class, d⁻ = ||f(a) − f(n)||₂ is the distance to a negative n of another class, f is the embedding network, and margin is a chosen gap, often 0.2 to 0.5. A triplet already well separated gives zero.

blocks.text: Ranking loss is the general name for losses that only order distances. Vision Transformers cut the image into 16 × 16 patches, flatten each into a vector, add position embeddings, and let self-attention mix all patches. Swin Transformers restrict attention to shifted local windows. Only a few universities teach these; the convolution ideas above still apply.

examples.question: AlexNet layer 1: input 227×227×3, 96 filters of size 11×11, stride 4, no padding. (a) Find the output size. (b) Count the weights in this layer. (c) After a 3×3 max pool with stride 2, what is the map size?
steps: Write the side formula: n_out = ⌊(n + 2p − k) ÷ s⌋ + 1, with n = 227, k = 11, s = 4, p = 0.
216 ÷ 4 = 54 exactly, and 54 + 1 = 55. The output is 55 × 55 pixels with 96 channels, one per filter: 55 × 55 × 96.
Weights per filter: 11 × 11 × 3 = 363. Add one bias per filter: 364.
examples.answer: The convolution output is 55 × 55 × 96, layer 1 holds 34,944 parameters, and the pooled map is 27 × 27 × 96.
examples.check:
n, k, s, p = 227, 11, 4, 0
out = (n + 2 * p - k) // s + 1
params = (k * k * 3 + 1) * 96
pool = (out - 3) // 2 + 1
print(out)
print(params)
print(pool)

traps: Pooling and output sizes floor, they do not round. 55 with a 3 × 3 pool and stride 2 gives ⌊52 ÷ 2⌋ + 1 = 27, not 26 or 28.
A shortcut cannot add tensors of different shapes. A channel change or stride-2 block needs a 1 × 1 convolution projection, a step exams drop.
Count the bias once per filter. AlexNet layer 1 has (11 × 11 × 3 + 1) × 96 = 34,944 weights, not 34,848.
VGG's parameters are in the classifier, not the convolutions. Blaming the 3 × 3 kernels for the huge parameter count is the wrong answer.
Triplet loss is max(0, d⁺ − d⁻ + margin). A well-separated triplet gives 0, not a negative number.

quiz.q: How many convolution and fully connected layers does AlexNet have, and how many output classes?
quiz.a: 5 convolution and 3 fully connected layers; 1000 classes.

quiz.q: What does weight sharing mean in a convolution layer?
quiz.a: One filter reuses the same k × k × C weights at every position, so the layer stores far fewer numbers than a fully connected layer of the same width.

quiz.q: Why does stacking convolution and pooling layers produce hierarchical features?
quiz.a: Pooling shrinks the map, so each deeper neuron covers a larger patch of the original image — edges first, then textures and parts, then whole objects.

quiz.q: Why is a residual block with F(x) = 0 easy to learn, and why does that help very deep networks?
quiz.a: Then y = x and the block is an identity. The optimiser only has to shrink the conv weights instead of learning an identity mapping from scratch, and gradients reach early layers through the shortcut.

quiz.q: A 56 × 56 × 64 input passes through 128 filters of 3 × 3, stride 1, padding 1. Find the output size and the number of weights in the layer.
A triplet has d⁺ = 0.4, d⁻ = 0.9, margin 0.3. Find the loss, then repeat with d⁻ = 0.5.
VGG-16 uses only 3 × 3 kernels yet has more parameters than AlexNet. Where do they sit, and why does this matter at inference?
quiz.a: About 102.8 million of roughly 138 million are in the first fully connected layer, fed by a 7 × 7 × 512 = 25,088-vector. The convolutions are small. VGG is therefore memory-heavy and slower than its convolution count suggests, so it is used more as a fixed feature extractor than as a deployable classifier.

beyond: Not for the exam. EfficientNet scales depth, width and resolution together with a compound coefficient; ConvNeXt rebuilds a ResNet block with transformer-era choices. Few people train from scratch on a small dataset — ImageNet pretrained weights plus fine-tuning are the default, which is why these backbones still matter. Search terms: transfer learning, compound scaling, ConvNeXt.
